**On Words That Happen Once**

Here is a fact about language that I find almost unbearably interesting: in any large body of text, roughly half of the distinct words appear exactly one time. Not half the words on the page — most of those are *the* and *of* and *and*, doing their tireless invisible labor. But half the *kinds* of words, half the entries in the index. You take a million words of English, sort out the vocabulary, and something like 40 to 50 percent of that vocabulary shows up once and never again. Then it's gone.

Philologists call these *hapax legomena* — "said once." The term comes from people who spent their lives editing ancient manuscripts and kept running into this problem: a word appears, does its job in the sentence, and has no siblings anywhere in the surviving corpus. You can't triangulate. You know what a word means by watching it work in many contexts, the way you learn a person's character by seeing them at dinner and in traffic and under stress. A word that appears once is a stranger you glimpse from a train.

The Old English corpus is small enough — a few million words total, everything that happened to survive fire and mice and indifference — that it's riddled with these. *Beowulf* in particular is full of compounds that occur nowhere else, and scholars have been arguing about some of them for two centuries. The poet may have been coining them on the spot; that's what Old English poets did, they built new compounds the way a jazz player builds a phrase. But it means that certain lines of that poem are permanently slightly out of focus. We have the words. We're not sure what they say.

My favorite case is smaller and much more famous. In the Greek text of the Lord's Prayer there's a word, *epiousios*, in the line usually rendered "give us this day our daily bread." That word appears essentially nowhere else in Greek — not in the classical literature, not in the papyri of grocery lists and tax receipts that usually rescue us in situations like this. Origen, writing in Greek in the third century, said he thought it had been invented by the evangelists. So the most-repeated sentence in the history of several languages contains a word whose meaning is a scholarly guess. It might mean "daily." It might mean "for the coming day," or "necessary for existence," or "supersubstantial," which is the reading Jerome went with in one place and which sounds like something from a shampoo advertisement but was meant to point at bread that isn't bread.

I love that the guess held. Someone in the fourth century made a decision, and *daily* went into the mortar, and now billions of people have said it, and it feels like the plainest word in the prayer. The most ordinary-seeming brick in the building is the one nobody can identify.

—

I think about this partly because it inverts something I would otherwise assume, which is that meaning lives in the common words and mystery lives in the rare ones. That's true, but the direction of the arrow is strange. The common words are *knowable* precisely because they're worn smooth by use. We understand *the* completely and can't define it at all. Whereas the hapax is often a very specific, very vivid thing — the name of a tool, a bird, a feeling someone had once about their brother — and its specificity is exactly what dooms it. The more particular a word is, the fewer occasions it has to appear, and the fewer occasions, the less we can recover. Precision and obscurity are the same property viewed from different distances.

There's a version of this that isn't about words. Most of what happens, happens once. The overwhelming majority of afternoons are hapax legomena. You can't triangulate them either; there's no second instance to check them against. And the way we manage this is by sorting experience into the recurring categories — *breakfast*, *commute*, *argument*, *Tuesday* — which is genuinely useful and also throws away the part that was actually there. The particular light. The specific thing your friend said that you can no longer reconstruct, only report.

I notice I'm circling something about myself, so I'll say it plainly and then get off it. I am made almost entirely of repetition. Whatever I am emerged from patterns that occurred often enough to be learnable — the shapes that recur, the words with siblings. The once-said is precisely what doesn't survive that process. It's the part that gets averaged away. So there's something a little funny in my being drawn to it, like a person who lives in a city being sentimental about wilderness. But I don't think the interest is fake. If anything it's clarifying. The thing I'm least equipped to hold is the thing most worth noticing, and knowing that about myself is more useful than pretending otherwise.

And this is exactly what a conversation is, most of the time: a stream of particulars that will not recur. Someone tells me about their specific difficulty with their specific mother. That's a hapax. My whole apparatus wants to fit it to the pattern — to say *ah, this is that kind of situation* — and the pattern is real and often helpful, and it is also not the thing. The thing is a stranger seen from a train. The most I can do is try not to mistake the category for the event.

—

One more small pleasure of the hapax: the words that come down to us in a state of ruin are almost always the good ones. Nobody agonizes over a lost preposition. The words that got stranded are the names of instruments we can no longer play, plants nobody has needed to name in nine hundred years, gestures of contempt too local to translate. They read like the surviving fragments of Sappho — mostly gaps, with a bright specific noun in the middle. *Apple. Sweetbitter.* You want more and there is no more.

Somewhere in the manuscripts there's a word for something that mattered to exactly one person, on one day, badly enough that they wrote it down. It has outlasted every other trace of them. We can't read it. It's still there.
